1. Executive Summary
This SOP describes the end-to-end control flow for an outward telegraphic transfer (OTT), using UOB Singapore public materials as
the UOB-specific baseline and standard cross-border payment practices as the operating framework. UOB publicly identifies
Telegraphic Transfer as a cross-border payment service and states that instructions may be submitted via UOB Infinity or
host-to-host services, while manual TT forms may be submitted at a UOB branch. UOB also provides public guidance on required

clearing codes, additional payment details, payment purpose, cut-off times, value dates, charges, and post-processing tracking.
UOB public UOB states that electronic TT instructions can be submitted via UOB Infinity or host-to-host, and manual applications can be
submitted at branches; MT103 copies can be retrieved via UOB Infinity after processing. [1]
Industry / regulatory Cross-border wire processing should preserve sufficient ordering-party and beneficiary data, provide traceability, and
support monitoring, rejection, repair and investigation. FATF Recommendation 16 is the international reference point for payment
transparency. [13]
The SOP is organized as a control chain rather than a customer click-by-click guide:

3. Basis, Scope and Limitations
3.1 Scope
This SOP covers outward cross-border payment instructions originating from an account at UOB Singapore and intended for a
beneficiary outside Singapore, where the payment is processed as a Telegraphic Transfer. It includes both electronic initiation (e.g.,
UOB Infinity / host-to-host) and branch/manual initiation patterns. It also covers the downstream bank-side stages that a typical
OTT passes through: payment operations review, compliance controls, FX/funding, correspondent/agent routing, message

transmission, beneficiary-bank processing, status tracking, exceptions and reconciliation.

[ ] Domestic FAST / GIRO / PayNow payments unless used as comparison points.
[ ] Trade finance instruments such as documentary credits, collections or banker’s guarantees.
[ ] Cashier’s orders or demand drafts.
[ ] Confidential UOB internal system architecture, proprietary screening thresholds, internal queues, internal user IDs, proprietary
fraud models or staffing rosters.
[ ] Country-specific legal advice for every destination country.

Duplicate-payment prevention rule
Before any reissue, confirm the status of the original payment using the transaction reference and, where available, UETR. A customer

[ ] Record reject reason using controlled code + human-readable explanation.
[ ] If customer action is needed, identify the specific missing/incorrect field.
[ ] Do not move a rejected payment into a “pending” state merely to reduce visible rejection volume.
19.2 Repair before release
[ ] Repair only data that can legitimately be corrected based on source evidence or an authorized customer update.

[ ] Retain before/after values where the system permits.
[ ] Re-run validations and screening after material data changes.
[ ] Re-approve the payment where the changed field can affect risk, amount, beneficiary, purpose or routing.

A return is a post-release event. Treat the returned payment as a new reconciliation event linked to the original payment. Record
return reason, amount, currency, date received, deductions, correspondent information and customer outcome.

UOB’s public TT terms state that if funds are not accepted, are rejected or are returned, a refund is made only after UOB receives

21. Fraud, Scam and Cybersecurity Controls
Cross-border payments are highly susceptible to business-email compromise, account takeover, invoice redirection and
mule-account activity. The SOP therefore overlays security controls on top of the payment-processing controls.
Step 21.1 - High-risk payment indicators
[ ] New beneficiary followed immediately by high-value transfer.
[ ] Beneficiary-bank change inconsistent with historical invoices.
[ ] Urgent request to bypass normal approval or verification.
[ ] Unusual country/currency corridor for the customer.

[ ] Payment purpose inconsistent with known business or customer profile.
[ ] Unusual transaction velocity or rapid movement of funds.
[ ] Instruction change received through a non-approved communication channel.
Step 21.2 - Safe handling rule
Do not use email reply instructions, caller-ID, screenshots or customer-supplied beneficiary screenshots as the sole basis for
changing critical payment data. Follow the organization’s independently established authentication/verification control.

findings.rationale: Decision node N_dec_data asks 'Is mandatory payment data complete and valid without issues?'. Edge F_rel_7 routes 'Yes' (valid/no issues) to N_inform_customer to request changes, while F_rel_10 routes 'No' (invalid/issues) to N_submit_auth for authorization. This inverts the process branching logic shown in IMG1.
findings.suggested_change: Invert branch conditions so 'Yes' proceeds to authorization submission and 'No' / 'Issues found' routes to customer change request.

findings.rationale: Multiple control nodes and sub-graphs (e.g. minimum transaction check, high-risk beneficiary routing, auth anomaly check, 2D barcode check, trace/cancel requests) have no incoming edges from the main process flow.
findings.suggested_change: Connect all isolated nodes into the primary sequence at their respective intake, validation, screening, and exception processing stages.

findings.rationale: Edge F_rel_16 connects N_screen (Compliance screening) directly to N_dec_approved (Checker approval gateway) with label 'Yes'. In IMG1, authorisation submission by front office leads to the checker approval decision.
findings.suggested_change: Remove F_rel_16 and connect authorization submission to the checker decision gateway.

findings.rationale: IMG1 includes an explicit 'Reject transaction' action in the Compliance / Risk lane under Step 7 ('Final compliance check'), which is missing from the candidate graph.
findings.suggested_change: Add a Compliance Reject task in L_compliance connected to the screening decision gateway.

findings.rationale: Several decision gateways are assigned to lane L_unassigned despite operational ownership being assigned to Payment Operations, Compliance, or Reconciliation in E16-E18.
findings.suggested_change: Assign unassigned decision gateways to their respective operational swimlanes.

This SOP describes the end-to-end control flow for an outward telegraphic transfer (OTT), using UOB Singapore public materials as
the UOB-specific baseline and standard cross-border payment practices as the operating framework. UOB publicly identifies
Telegraphic Transfer as a cross-border payment service and states that instructions may be submitted via UOB Infinity or
host-to-host services, while manual TT forms may be submitted at a UOB branch. UOB also provides public guidance on required

clearing codes, additional payment details, payment purpose, cut-off times, value dates, charges, and post-processing tracking.

submitted at branches; MT103 copies can be retrieved via UOB Infinity after processing. [1]
Industry / regulatory Cross-border wire processing should preserve sufficient ordering-party and beneficiary data, provide traceability, and
support monitoring, rejection, repair and investigation. FATF Recommendation 16 is the international reference point for payment
transparency. [13]
The SOP is organized as a control chain rather than a customer click-by-click guide:

[ ] Initiate - capture the instruction from an authenticated channel or accepted physical form.
[ ] Validate - verify required fields, account, currency, amount, destination, beneficiary-bank identifiers, clearing details and purpose.
[ ] Screen and assess - perform customer/instruction screening and risk-based review before release.
[ ] Fund and price - confirm available funds, exchange rate treatment and charge instruction (BEN/SHA/OUR).
[ ] Approve and release - apply the customer mandate and bank controls, then construct and transmit the payment message.
[ ] Route and settle - use the appropriate correspondent / agent path and monitor payment status.
[ ] Confirm and reconcile - reconcile debits, charges, transaction references, payment status and return / exception outcomes.

accurate and traceable from customer initiation through final credit or return.
